Sanguine means optimistic — specifically, feeling cheerfully confident that things will turn out well, even when the situation is uncertain or difficult.

But it's not quite the same as simply saying "optimistic." Here's the key difference:

Being optimistic just means you expect good things to happen. Being sanguine adds a layer of calm, almost breezy confidence to that. A sanguine person doesn't anxiously hope things will work out — they genuinely and comfortably expect them to, and they carry that expectation with a relaxed, upbeat attitude. There's a quietness to sanguine optimism. It's less "I really hope this goes well!" and more "I believe this will go fine."
A Feeling, Not Just a Thought

What makes "sanguine" rich and precise is that it describes both an attitude and an emotional state at once.

A person who is sanguine about something isn't just intellectually predicting a good outcome — they feel good about it. They're not worried. They're not wringing their hands. They're composed, positive, and forward-looking.

This is why "sanguine" is often used in formal, professional, or serious contexts — situations where many people would be anxious or pessimistic, but where the sanguine person remains genuinely upbeat.

These examples will show you how the word feels in real use:

  • "The coach was sanguine about the team's chances, despite losing three players to injury."
    → The coach was confident and calm, not panicking, believing the team would still do well.
  • "Not everyone is sanguine about the future of the economy."
    → Not everyone is optimistic or confident that the economy will improve.
  • "She remained sanguine throughout the long and difficult negotiations."
    → She stayed positive and composed even when the talks were tough.
  • "He was sanguine that a solution would be found."
    → He was quietly sure a solution was coming.

Notice the word "remained" in the third example — "sanguine" is very commonly used in contexts where there is pressure, difficulty, or bad news, and someone maintains their positive outlook despite it. That contrast is where the word really shines.

Yes — and this is an important nuance. Sometimes "sanguine" carries a subtle suggestion that the optimism is perhaps too easy, or not fully justified by the facts.

For example:

  • "The government seems sanguine about the risks — perhaps too much so."

Here, calling someone sanguine gently implies they might be underestimating the problem, being naively cheerful, or turning a blind eye to warning signs. The word doesn't always mean this, but the context can push it in that direction.

So the full emotional range of "sanguine" runs from:

  • ✅ Admirably calm and confident in difficulty — to —
  • ⚠️ Unrealistically or dangerously optimistic

In most cases, whether it's meant positively or critically will be clear from the sentence around it.

"Sanguine" has a second, separate meaning: it can describe a deep blood-red color. You might see this in formal or artistic writing — "a sanguine sky at dusk" or "sanguine robes." In art, a sanguine is specifically a drawing made in red chalk.

This meaning is much rarer in everyday speech. If you encounter it outside of art or heraldry, you'll almost certainly know from context that color is being described.

This one is fascinating and actually explains why the word came to mean optimistic in the first place.

For over a thousand years, doctors and philosophers believed that a person's personality and health were shaped by four bodily fluids called humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. Each humor corresponded to a personality type.

A person whose dominant humor was blood was called sanguine. And the sanguine personality type was considered the happiest, most sociable, most cheerful of the four. Sanguine people were described as:

  • Energetic and enthusiastic
  • Sociable and talkative
  • Naturally optimistic and confident
  • Warm and pleasure-loving

This is the direct ancestor of the modern meaning. The "sanguine temperament" was the happy, upbeat, people-loving type — and that cheerful, confident optimism is exactly what the word still means today.

You won't hear "sanguine" used this way (as a personality temperament) in modern everyday language, but if you encounter it in historical texts, psychology discussions, or literature, this is what it refers to.

SituationWhat "sanguine" means
Everyday modern useOptimistically confident, especially in difficult circumstances
Used with mild criticismPerhaps unrealistically or too easily optimistic
In art or formal writingDeep blood-red in color
In historical or psychological contextsA cheerful, sociable, optimistic personality type

The single sentence to carry with you: Sanguine means calmly and confidently optimistic, especially when others might not be.
